claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by kinetic control of atomic diffusion at the nanoparticle surface.
Rapid processing minimizes coalescence-driven surface diffusion.
Surface diffusion causes segregation of low-surface-energy elements.
Kinetic trapping preserves a homogeneous multimetal distribution before thermodynamic surface-energy minimization produces phase separation.
The relevant precursor system can have a near-equimolar distribution of Au, Co, Cu, Ni, and Pt.
The initial Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles have a kinetically trapped FCC structure.
Controlled rapid thermal profiles can minimize nanoparticle coalescence and associated collective atomic diffusion.
Processing for less time than is required to reach thermodynamic equilibrium enables kinetic control to dominate.
A surface-energy gradient drives the lowest-surface-energy elements toward the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu segregate to the surface of heated Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu surface migration is driven by minimization of the nanoparticle's overall free energy.
Coalescence and collective diffusion promote Au/Cu segregation and phase separation during conventional thermal treatment.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles should have a more homogeneous core and surface elemental distribution than conventionally processed nanoparticles.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles should exhibit less Au/Cu surface enrichment and less phase separation than the unchanged baseline.
Heating Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles progressively produces coalescence, Au/Cu surface segregation, and phase separation.
At sufficiently high temperature, Au and Cu can be lost from the nanoparticles.
The proposed kinetic-control mechanism particularly applies to noble metal–based nanoparticle systems containing at least five interacting elements.
The mechanism should not apply when processing permits equilibrium or when forces unrelated to surface-diffusion kinetics dominate.
